propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: The appellant is a citizen of Haiti.
propositions.quote: The appellant XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Haiti.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant is a citizen of Haiti.

propositions.text: The appellant fears being killed or mistreated in Haiti by several gangs in Cité Soleil, especially two gang leaders.
propositions.quote: The appellant claims that he fears being killed or mistreated in Haiti by several gangs in Cité Soleil, and in particular by two gang leaders whom he calls XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: He fears for his life because he fired one gang leader's brother and refused to hire people recommended by gang leaders for a UNOPS shelter project.
propositions.quote: He fears for his life because he allegedly fired XXXX XXXX brother and refused to hire people recommended by Cité Soleil's gang leaders for the shelter project carried out as part of the United Nations Office for Project Services' (UNOPS) operations.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant claims fear of harm from gangs in Haiti due to employment disputes related to a UNOPS shelter project.

propositions.text: The appellant left Haiti in 2013 for the US, returned there, then entered Canada and filed a refugee claim in 2017.
propositions.quote: Fearing for his life, the appellant left Haiti in 2013 for the United States. He returned to the United States. He entered Canada and filed his refugee protection claim on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant left Haiti in 2013, returned to the US, then entered Canada and filed a refugee claim in 2017.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claim on June 13, 2019, due to appellant's lack of credibility on central elements.
propositions.quote: On June 13, 2019, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the claim on the grounds that the appellant was not credible on central elements of his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the appellant's claim in 2019 for lack of credibility on key elements.

propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal and find the RPD was correct that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in determining that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, agreeing with the RPD's decision that the appellant is not a refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The appellant submits four new documents.
propositions.quote: The appellant submits four new documents.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submits four new documents as evidence.

propositions.text: Under the Act, evidence can only be allowed if it arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably have been presented before.
propositions.quote: Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the Act), I can only allow evidence: i. that arose after the RPD rendered its decision; ii. that was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented to the RPD before the decision was rendered.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Act's criteria for allowing new evidence after the RPD decision.

propositions.text: If evidence meets these criteria, it must be assessed for newness, credibility, and relevance before admission.
propositions.quote: If the evidence fulfills one or more of these requirements, I must decide whether the evidence is new, credible and relevant before admitting it.

paragraphs.summary: The court must assess new evidence for newness, credibility, and relevance before admitting it.

propositions.text: The appellant says the new documents show people want to hurt him and are looking for him.
propositions.quote: According to the appellant, these documents show that people want to hurt him and that they are looking for him.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the new documents show threats against him and that people seek him.

propositions.text: The first new document is a 2019 lease agreement, almost illegible, predating the RPD decision and known before it.
propositions.quote: The first document, which is entitled [translation] "lease agreement," is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. I note that this document is almost illegible. The document predates the RPD's decision and contains information about incidents before that decision.

propositions.text: The appellant could have presented this lease agreement to the RPD but did not explain why he did not.
propositions.quote: At all times before the rejection of the refugee protection claim, the appellant could have informed the RPD that he had such a document in his possession, but he failed to do so. The appellant provides no explanation as to why this document was not reasonably available or why he could not reasonably have been expected to file it in the circumstances, before the decision was rendered.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the first document is a 2019 lease agreement predating the RPD decision and was available but not presented by the appellant.

propositions.text: The lease agreement does not meet the Act's requirements and is not accepted as evidence.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I am of the view that this document does not comply with the requirements set out in subsection 110(4) of the Act because it does not refer to incidents that arose after the RPD's rejection of the refugee protection claim, and it was normally accessible to the appellant, who could have presented it to the RPD in the circumstances at the time the RPD rejected the refugee protection claim. Since it does not comply with the requirements of the Act, I am not required to address the relevance or credibility of this document. Consequently, the evidence is not accepted.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the lease agreement as evidence because it does not meet the Act's requirements.

propositions.text: The other three documents, though dated after the RPD decision, fail the Singh jurisprudential test for admissibility.
propositions.quote: Despite the fact that those three other documents are dated after the date on which the RPD decision was signed, and thus comply with the wording of subsection 110(4) regarding the deadline, and despite the fact that they arose after the rejection of the claim, they fail the jurisprudential analysis test in Singh.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the other three documents fail the Singh test despite being dated after the RPD decision.

propositions.text: The first of the three documents is a medical certificate with spelling errors, missing accents, written in English, and unsigned, making it not credible.
propositions.quote: The first document, a medical certificate from the XXXX Hospital, includes numerous spelling mistakes. I note that several accents are missing and that on the certificate's header, it is written 'Hospital' and not 'Hôpital' and that it states "phone" whereas the official languages of Haiti are French and Creole. I also note that all the accents are missing, including the diaeresis on Haïti, and that the word thoracique is spelled 'toraxique' and is also missing an s at the end. I would have expected the medical words to be written by the medical specialist and the document to be written in one of the country's official languages. I also note that the document is not signed. Thus, looking at the medical certificate itself, I find this document not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the medical certificate not credible due to errors, language issues, and lack of signature.

propositions.text: The second document is a police complaint repeating the attestation, describing threats and vandalism at a relative's home, but is not credible or relevant given the medical certificate's lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The second document is a complaint to Haiti's national police, which almost reiterates the content of his attestation. This document states that the authorities went to XXXX XXXX residence and that three men showed up at her home and beat her, asking where the appellant was. They also allegedly threatened her and vandalized her house before leaving. In light of the medical certificate's lack of credibility, I am of the opinion that this document is not credible in terms of its content and therefore not relevant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the police complaint not credible or relevant due to the medical certificate's lack of credibility.

propositions.text: The appellant's affidavit is inadmissible as it merely reiterates previous evidence and adds no new relevant or credible information.
propositions.quote: The affidavit presented by the appellant is not admissible as new evidence since the affidavit is nothing more than a reiteration of the memorandum filed and does not shed additional new, relevant and credible light on the debate raised before the RPD. Consequently, it is not admissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's affidavit inadmissible as it repeats prior evidence without adding new relevant or credible information.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the four new documents inadmissible under subsection 110(4) of the Act.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) finds that these four documents are not admissible as evidence under subsection 110(4) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the four new documents inadmissible under the Act.

propositions.text: My role is to review all evidence and determine if the RPD's decision is correct; the key issue is credibility.
propositions.quote: My role is to review all the evidence and to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.3 The determinative issue is credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD decision is correct, focusing on credibility.

propositions.text: The appellant alleges the RPD erred in fact and law, giving unreasonable, unsupported reasons and errors of law.
propositions.quote: The appellant alleges that the RPD erred in fact and in law in that the reasons given by the Board are unreasonable, unsupported by the evidence and constitute errors of law.

propositions.text: The RPD based its decision on irrelevant and non-determinative elements.
propositions.quote: The RPD based its decision on irrelevant and non-determinative elements for the outcome of the appellant's claimed rights.

propositions.text: The RPD draws negative inferences on non-determinative and less relevant elements.
propositions.quote: The RPD draws negative inferences on elements that are non-determinative and even less relevant to the appellant's claim.

propositions.text: The RPD does not clearly establish relevant elements or their probative value.
propositions.quote: The RPD does not seem to clearly establish what the relevant elements of this case are and what probative value to give to them.

propositions.text: The RPD does not clearly explain how it concludes no risk of persecution exists.
propositions.quote: The RPD does not clearly establish how it concludes that there is no risk of persecution, with respect to the fear of being killed or seriously injured in Haiti.

propositions.text: The RPD's decision lacks consistency and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD's decision lacks consistency and intelligibility.

propositions.text: The RPD improperly referred to evidence supporting its conclusions without mentioning contrary evidence; evidence must be weighed as a whole.
propositions.quote: The RPD should not have referred to certain pieces of evidence that support its conclusions, without also referring to contrary evidence. Moreover, the assessment of all the evidence implies that it must be weighed as a whole and not some of it considered in isolation from the rest of the evidence.

propositions.text: The appellant's testimony has no contradictions on crucial facts.
propositions.quote: The appellant's testimony does not present any contradictions on crucial facts forming the basis of the refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by not considering all evidence provided.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in its assessment of facts and did not take into account all the evidence provided.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in assessing risks to the appellant, which are real given Haiti's violent situation.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in its assessment of the risks the appellant faces should he leave Canada, and they are unfounded given the violent situation in Haiti.

propositions.text: The RPD erred notably and obviously in assessing facts and evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in a notable and obvious manner in its assessment of the facts and evidence on the record.

propositions.text: The RPD erred regarding appellant's lack of subjective fear and prospective risk; objective risk from evidence supports appellant's testimony and shows risk exists.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred with respect to the appellant's lack of subjective fear and the lack of prospective risk. However, the objective risk of threat to the appellant's life that emerges from the documentary evidence and supports the appellant's testimony is sufficient to determine that the RPD's findings are unreasonable and erroneous in fact and in law. The appellant is indeed at risk and cannot receive adequate protection in Haiti.

propositions.text: The RPD failed to consider all evidence, making its decision unjustified and unintelligible.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in failing to consider all of the evidence and, as a result, its decision lacks justification and intelligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleges multiple errors by the RPD including irrelevant reasoning, failure to consider evidence, and unreasonable findings on risk and credibility.

propositions.text: The appellant did not support his arguments with specific evidence or identify where errors occurred during the hearing.
propositions.quote: I note that even though the appellant raised the arguments above, he did not support them with specific evidence stating the errors made in the decision and indicating where the problems arose during the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant failed to support his arguments with specific evidence or identify errors during the hearing.

propositions.text: Paragraph 3(3)(g) of RAD Rules requires appellant's memorandum to include full and detailed submissions on specified points.
propositions.quote: paragraph 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) requires the appellant's memorandum to include full and detailed submissions regarding i. the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, ii. where the errors are located in the written reasons for the RDP's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the RPD's hearing, iii. how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant, iv. the decision the appellant wants the Division to make, and v. why the Division should hold a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the Act if the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held.

paragraphs.summary: The court states RAD Rule 3(3)(g) requires appellant's memorandum to include detailed submissions on errors, their location, evidence, desired decision, and hearing request.

propositions.text: The appeal does not comply with RAD Rules 3(3)(g)(i) and (ii) because appellant fails to specify problematic sections or explain errors.
propositions.quote: I consider that this appeal does not comply with subparagraphs 3(3)(g)(i) and 3(3)(g)(ii) of the RAD Rules because the appellant does not state in the memorandum the sections of the RPD's reasons he considers problematic and does not fully explain why the conclusions are problematic or indicate the specific errors he has identified in that section.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appeal non-compliant with RAD Rules 3(3)(g)(i) and (ii) due to lack of specific error identification by appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant's memorandum lacks sufficient arguments or analysis explaining why issues raised caused erroneous findings of fact.
propositions.quote: there is an absence or insufficiency of arguments or analysis as to why these issues raised resulted in erroneous findings of fact.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's memorandum insufficiently argues why issues raised caused erroneous findings of fact.

propositions.text: Appeal process is party driven; RAD is not to supplement weaknesses or create new ideas for appellants.
propositions.quote: It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it, or, for that matter, of the refugee protection claim presented in the first place. It is not its role to come up with new ideas that might assist appellants in succeeding with their appeal and, ultimately, their refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Justice LeBlanc that the appeal process is party driven and RAD must not supplement appeal weaknesses or create new ideas.

propositions.text: RAD Rules 3(3)(g)(i) and (ii) requirements are not met, but court conducted independent assessment of RPD record and evidence.
propositions.quote: The RAD considers that the requirements of subparagraphs 3(3)(g)(i) and 3(3)(g)(ii) of the RAD Rules are not met. Nevertheless, I conducted an independent assessment of the RPD record, including listening to the recording of the RPD's hearing, and reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD Rules 3(3)(g)(i) and (ii) unmet but independently assessed the RPD record and evidence.

propositions.text: RPD found appellant's allegations of harm by gangs not credible for multiple reasons including omissions, inconsistencies, contradictions, and inconsistent behaviour.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the appellant's allegations of harm at the hands of the gangs and the two gang leaders he calls XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX in his birth region in Haiti were not credible for the following reasons: • Omission, in the written account of his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), of the allegation of death threats after he left Haiti. • Inconsistency between his oral evidence and the written account in his BOC Form regarding the threats coming from the XXXX family. • Contradiction about where he learned about the threats previously mentioned. • Lack of a reasonable explanation regarding requests and threats from individuals associated with XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX and the family relationship. • Behaviour inconsistent with his alleged fear of losing his life, as he returned to live in Haiti at the same home in XXXX 2013 after leaving for the United States in XXXX 2013 because he feared for his life in XXXX 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found appellant's harm allegations not credible due to omissions, inconsistencies, contradictions, and inconsistent behaviour.

propositions.text: After reviewing evidence and hearing, court finds no significant error in RPD decision and agrees credibility is determinative issue.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed all the evidence, including the documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP), and having listened to the recording of the RPD's hearing, I conclude that there is no significant error in the RPD's decision. The determinative issue is that of the appellant's credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant confirmed BOC Form contents but omissions and contradictions undermined credibility; explanations unsatisfactory.
propositions.quote: At the beginning of the hearing, as is appropriate, the principal appellant was questioned about the truthfulness of the contents of his BOC Form, and he confirmed that the contents were correct. The RPD identified omissions between his testimony and the BOC Form, and the explanations for them were not satisfactory.

propositions.text: Appellant's inconsistent behaviour and failure to apply for asylum in US further undermine credibility.
propositions.quote: I am also of the view that the appellant's actions are inconsistent, in the absence of satisfactory explanations, with the behaviour of someone who is fleeing from his attackers, and this consequently undermines his credibility. After my own analysis of the evidence, I note that the appellant did not apply for asylum during his stay in the United States, even though he testified that he left Haiti in XXXX 2013 because he feared for his life, while considering the fact that he returned to Haiti willingly, which further undermines his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no significant error in RPD decision, agrees credibility is key, and notes appellant's omissions, contradictions, and inconsistent behaviour undermine credibility.

propositions.text: RPD concluded appellant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that the appellant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found appellant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

propositions.text: Due to lack of specific submissions and references, RAD is not required to proceed further.
propositions.quote: Due to the lack of submissions to address specific errors made by the RPD, and the lack of references to the location of the errors in the RPD decision and/or the audio recording of the hearing, the RAD is not required to go any further.

propositions.text: Appellant is represented by lawyer knowledgeable of RAD Rules and resources are available to assist appeals.
propositions.quote: In addition, I note that the appellant is represented by a lawyer who should have a good knowledge of the RAD Rules. I would also point out that there are resources available to appellants and representatives alike to make and prepare their appeals: information sessions on how to appeal to the RAD, and specifically how to perfect an appeal to the RAD, an online Appellant's Record template that sets out all the information that must be provided on appeal, and the Appellant's Guide, which is accessible in 16 languages on the RAD's webpage.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD need not proceed further due to lack of specific submissions; appellant has lawyer and resources to assist appeal.

propositions.text: Lack of compliance with RAD Rule 3(3)(g) forces RAD to guess potential RPD errors, which it must not do.
propositions.quote: A lack of compliance with RAD Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules leaves the RAD in a position that it must "guess" at the potential errors that the RPD may have committed.

propositions.text: Dhillon: RAD must not supplement appeal weaknesses or create new ideas to assist appellants.
propositions.quote: As stated in Dhillon, "It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it, or, for that matter, of the refugee protection claim presented in the first place. It is also not its role to come up with new ideas that might assist appellants in succeeding with their appeal and, ultimately, their refugee claim."

propositions.text: Ghauri: Appellant must establish RPD erred to justify RAD intervention; failure to specify errors is at appellant's peril.
propositions.quote: Justice Gleeson remarks, in obiter in Ghauri that "... it is the appellant's responsibility, not the RAD's to establish that the RPD erred in a way that justifies the interventions of the RAD." The court concluded that "appellants before the RAD that fail to specify where and how the RPD erred do so at their own peril."

paragraphs.summary: The court cites case law that RAD must not guess errors and appellants must specify RPD errors to justify RAD intervention.

propositions.text: Murugesu: RAD must not supplement appeal weaknesses.
propositions.quote: Justice Fothergill states in Murugesu "It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it,"

propositions.text: Liu: RAD Rule 3(3)(g) places onus on appellant to identify errors and their location in RPD decision.
propositions.quote: in Liu, the Federal Court states that "Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules, SOR/2012-257, places the onus on an appellant to identify in his or her submissions to the RAD the errors that form the grounds of appeal," in addition to the location of the errors in the RPD's decision.

propositions.text: Dahal: RAD's brief review of full RPD record to ensure no unraised errors does not make decision vulnerable to review.
propositions.quote: As stated by Chief Justice Crampton in Dahal with respect to RAD Rules 3(3)(g)(i) and (ii): ... In essence, what the RAD did was to briefly review the full record before the RPD, to ensure that it did not make any errors that were not identified by the Applicants. By simply satisfying itself that no such additional errors were made, the RAD's decision should not become vulnerable to being set aside on judicial review, based solely on its general concurrence with findings made by the RPD in respect of matters that were not raised on appeal by the Applicants.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites cases emphasizing appellant's burden to identify errors and RAD's limited role in reviewing unraised errors.

propositions.text: RAD is required to focus on specific errors alleged by appellant against RPD.
propositions.quote: In my view, this makes it clear that the RAD is required to focus on the specific errors that an appellant has alleged have been made by the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes RAD must focus on specific errors alleged by appellant against RPD.

propositions.text: Court independently assessed evidence and finds RPD accurately restated appellant's testimony and credibility assessment is correct.
propositions.quote: I have conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence before the RPD in relation to the errors raised by the appellant. However, having listened to the audio recording of the RPD hearing, I find that the RPD accurately restated the appellant's testimony in this regard. I have also read the NDP with respect to the availability of state protection in Haiti, and I agree with the RPD's credibility assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The court independently assessed evidence and agrees with RPD's accurate restatement of testimony and credibility assessment.

propositions.text: Appellant did not establish on balance of probabilities that he faces danger of torture, risk to life, cruel treatment, or persecution on Convention grounds if returned to Haiti.
propositions.quote: In light of all the above, I am of the opinion that the appellant did not establish that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he return to Haiti. I also conclude that the appellant did not demonstrate that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on one of the Convention grounds, namely, membership in a particular social group, should he return to Haiti.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes appellant failed to prove risk of torture, life risk, cruel treatment, or persecution on Convention grounds if returned to Haiti.

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed and RPD's determination that appellant is neither Convention refugee nor person in need of protection is confirmed.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms RPD's determination appellant is neither Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.

propositions.text: The RAD briefly reviewed the full record before the RPD to ensure no errors were missed by the Applicants.
propositions.quote: In essence, what the RAD did was to briefly review the full record before the RPD, to ensure that it did not make any errors that were not identified by the Applicants.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD briefly reviewed the full record before the RPD to ensure no errors were missed by the Applicants, says the court.

propositions.text: The RAD's decision should not be set aside on judicial review just because it agreed with RPD findings not challenged by Applicants.
propositions.quote: By simply satisfying itself that no such additional errors were made, the RAD's decision should not become vulnerable to being set aside on judicial review, based solely on its general concurrence with findings made by the RPD in respect of matters that were not raised on appeal by the Applicants.

propositions.text: Rule 3(3)(g) requires an appellant to identify errors and their location in the RPD decision or hearing transcript.
propositions.quote: In my view, this would largely vitiate the purpose of Rule 3(3)(g) of the Rules, which requires an appellant to identify (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal (ii) where those errors are located in the RPD's decision, or in the transcript recording of its hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's decision should not be set aside for agreeing with unchallenged RPD findings and explains Rule 3(3)(g) requires appellants to identify errors and their location.
